ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Key federal laws include the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c 17, and its regulations, including the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations, SOR/2002-184. The Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46, addresses terrorist financing and sanctions-related offences; the United Nations Act, RSC 1985, c U-2, implements UN sanctions. Under the Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, ss. 2.1 and 21.1–21.3, federal corporations must identify individuals with significant control and file prescribed information. Alberta corporations are governed by the Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, including its register-of-individuals-with-significant-control requirements. Canada has no single comprehensive public UBO register applicable to all Alberta corporations. An Alberta ULC is not a federal CBCA corporation and should not be treated as subject to the CBCA filing regime.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Conduct risk-based identity verification, beneficial-ownership tracing to natural persons, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth review, and ongoing monitoring under the PCMLTFA and applicable regulations when acting as a reporting entity. Screen relevant parties against applicable Canadian sanctions lists and domestic law, UN Security Council sanctions, and OFAC lists where required by US nexus, counterparties, banks, or contractual policy. PEP and head-of-international-organization determinations, enhanced measures, approvals, and recordkeeping must follow the applicable PCMLTFA rules and the institution’s risk-based controls; OFAC screening is not a general Canadian statutory requirement absent a relevant nexus.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry services, accessed through an authorized Alberta registry agent; Alberta NUANS name-search services are used for named corporations
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names may be in English, French, or both, subject to statutory requirements and registry approval. A named Alberta ULC must include the prescribed liability designation, ordinarily “Unlimited Liability Corporation” or “ULC,” in accordance with Alberta law and registry practice. The name must be distinguishable and must not be prohibited, misleading, or likely to be confused with an existing name. Non-Latin characters and transliterations should be confirmed with the registry agent before filing.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Words implying a government connection, Crown status, or official endorsement without authorization
Bank, trust, trustee, fiduciary, or similar regulated-business terms where their use would imply an unlicensed regulated activity or require approval
Words implying a licensed profession or regulated financial institution without the required authorization
Obscene, misleading, or otherwise prohibited words
Restricted corporate designations or words requiring consent under applicable Alberta legislation
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Obtain an Alberta NUANS report and submit the proposed name through an authorized registry agent. Confirm the reservation expiry stated by the registry; a name reservation is generally valid for 90 days. If rejected, obtain the written reason, revise the name or provide supporting evidence of entitlement or consent, and resubmit. Request reconsideration or pursue any available statutory administrative review through the responsible Alberta registry authority where applicable; filing deadlines and review rights depend on the decision type. Do not use the rejected name unless approval is granted.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: An Alberta corporation must maintain a registered office in Alberta and a records office as required by the Business Corporations Act. A commercial registered-office provider may be acceptable if it satisfies statutory and service requirements, but a mailbox-only address may be inadequate. A virtual address does not replace operational substance, books and records, regulated-business premises, or a bank’s due-diligence requirements. The proposed trust-administration activity may require authorization under Alberta’s Loan and Trust Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c L-20, and related rules; obtain Alberta regulatory advice and written confirmation before offering services or representing that the corporation is licensed.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: No reliable public statutory percentage is available. Risk is elevated and unquantifiable for a proposed high-risk trust and asset-protection business; banks, regulators, tax authorities, and service providers may request site visits, records, management interviews, or evidence of genuine operations.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); principal online services are CRA My Business Account and Represent a Client. Alberta provincial corporate income tax is administered by the CRA under federal-provincial tax collection arrangements.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A material entity-form qualification applies: Alberta does not provide for incorporation as an unlimited liability corporation (ULC) under its Business Corporations Act. The stated Alberta ULC therefore cannot be treated as a valid Alberta-incorporated entity without confirmation of its actual jurisdiction and legal form. A foreign corporation carrying on business in Canada generally applies to the CRA for a Business Number (BN) and the required program accounts, including an RC corporate income tax account and, where applicable, an RT GST/HST account. Non-resident applicants may apply through CRA's applicable non-resident registration process and must provide formation documents, identifying information, Canadian business activity details, and authorized-representative information. Provincial extra-provincial registration may also be required. A BN or GST/HST registration does not validate an entity's claimed Alberta legal form.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canadian-resident corporations are generally subject to Canadian corporate income tax; Canada does not provide a general domestic check-the-box election to disregard a corporation or treat it as a partnership. A qualifying Canadian entity may make a U.S. entity-classification election under U.S. Treasury Regulations where eligible, but that election does not alter Canadian classification. ULCs formed in jurisdictions that authorize them are generally corporations for Canadian tax purposes. Cross-border hybrid mismatch rules, including relevant deduction denial and inclusion rules, may restrict tax benefits from a classification mismatch.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST); Alberta does not impose a provincial sales tax.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters for the small-supplier test, subject to statutory rules. Certain non-residents and other specified persons may be required to register without relying on the ordinary small-supplier threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no general federal real-time e-invoice clearance, API pre-approval, or digital-stamping mandate for ordinary GST supplies. GST registrants must issue invoices or receipts containing prescribed information where required and retain adequate records. Electronic records must remain accessible and satisfy CRA record-keeping requirements.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Qualifying exported goods are generally zero-rated when the statutory export conditions are met, including that the recipient is not resident in Canada and the supplier does not deliver or make the goods available in Canada to the recipient or a person designated by the recipient, subject to specific exceptions. Services supplied to non-residents may be zero-rated only where the applicable statutory category and exclusions are satisfied; non-resident status alone is insufficient. A registrant may generally claim input tax credits for eligible GST incurred in making zero-rated supplies, subject to documentation and statutory limitations.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Commercial invoice and purchase order or contract identifying the recipient, goods or services, and consideration
For goods, Canada Border Services Agency export declaration or other applicable export reporting evidence, together with carrier, bill of lading, airway bill, or delivery evidence establishing export
Evidence supporting the recipient's non-resident status and the location and nature of any services supplied
Supplier invoices and accounting records supporting claimed input tax credits
Foreign-exchange or remittance records where relevant to substantiate payment; Canada does not generally require an Inward Remittance Certificate as a condition of export zero-rating
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Canada has no general statutory foreign-exchange repatriation deadline for export proceeds. CRA may reassess improperly zero-rated supplies, deny related input tax credits, and assess interest and applicable penalties, including gross-negligence penalties where the statutory test is met. Customs reporting violations may attract separate penalties. The applicable limitation period and penalty depend on the facts and governing statute.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as the monetary and reserve-management authority, in functional partnership with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for prudential supervision of foreign-currency and derivative risk, the Department of Finance Canada for exchange-rate and external-sector policy, and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for cross-border monetary transaction monitoring. Canada has no dedicated Foreign Exchange Administration body; exchange controls are not exercised by the Bank of Canada, and the Canadian dollar has operated as a free-floating currency under a pure market-clearance regime since 1998.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada is an IMF Article VIII member (acceptance effective 25 March 1952) with full convertibility on both current account and capital account. There are no exchange-control authorizations, no repatriation quotas, no waiting periods, and no central-bank registration requirements for inbound or outbound transfers associated with discretionary trust administration. CAD is freely convertible into USD, EUR, GBP, CHF, JPY, and all deliverable currencies through Schedule I Canadian banks; capital movements for trust funding, discretionary distributions, offshore asset acquisitions, and profit remittance are unrestricted. The only material frictions are compliance-based rather than convertibility-based: KYC/UBO verification, FINTRAC suspicious-transaction reporting, the Part XIII 25% Canadian withholding tax on certain non-resident trust distributions (treaty-reducible), and CRS/FATCA classification obligations. For the Alberta ULC acting as fiduciary administrator, the practical hurdle to convertibility is the opening bank's internal country-risk policy toward FATF-monitored or sanctioned-adjacent jurisdictions, not any Canadian FX statute.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable. Canada imposes no statutory surrender timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, no export-proceeds banking rule, and no exchange repatriation ceiling under the Currency Act, the Bank of Canada Act, or the Investment Canada Act. Export receipts and inbound trust contributions in hard currency remain 100% freely disposable in the original denomination or may be converted into CAD at the corporate bank's interbank spread without regulatory declaration. The only voluntary compliance duties are: (a) reporting cross-border monetary transactions aggregating above C$10,000 in any FINTRAC reporting calendar to the Canada Border Services Agency and FINTRAC as required; (b) filing the CRA T2/T3/T106 schedules for trust distributions and cumulative FX gains or losses; and (c) maintaining the PCMLTFA seven-year record-keeping trail for each incoming payment, none of which constitutes a surrender or conversion obligation.

Operational Account + Trust Administration Settlement Account (CAD/USD dual-currency) + FX hedging line under TD Global FX desk

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Low-to-conditional. Canada has no EU-style Electronic Money Institution passport regime, and foreign digital EMIs (Wise, Revolut Business, Airwallex, Payoneer) cannot lawfully hold trust corpus, custody discretionary-asset-protection funds, or act as the primary clearing facility without either a provincial money-services licence or membership in Payments Canada. For the Alberta ULC, an offshore EMI is usable only as an auxiliary rail for low-value operational disbursements (legal fees, independent counsel retainers, auditor invoices) after negative-news screening, and must never be used for capital injections, settlor contributions, or beneficiary distributions exceeding C$10,000. The controlling legal constraint is that foreign EMIs are not registered as FINTRAC MSBs in Canada for fiduciary administration and will be declined by Tier-1 banks as verifiable counterparties; accordingly, all substantive cross-border liquidity must clear through Schedule I chartered-bank accounts or a FINTRAC-registered Canadian MSB.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: In-person physical appearance of at least one director, preferably the Chief Executive Officer or the designated Compliance Officer, is mandatory for the initial corporate onboarding at RBC, TD, and BMO, reflecting the high-risk fiduciary classification. CIBC and Scotiabank permit remote video onboarding, but only with enhanced due diligence, notarized identification, a bank referral from an existing private-banking relationship, and an interview with the institutional compliance committee. Because the ULC administers discretionary asset-protection trusts, the KYC interview must demonstrate the underlying trust deed, the protected-asset schedule, the settlor's source of wealth, the indemnity and professional-insurance cover, and the engagement of qualified Canadian legal counsel before any escrow account is opened. If all ULC directors are non-resident, the bank will require consular notarization of passports, an Alberta-registry-issued Certificate of Status, a board resolution certifying management independence and economic substance in Alberta, and a video conference with the relationship manager; some Tier-1 banks will waive physical appearance only where the beneficial owner holds pre-existing private-banking at the same institution in another G-7 jurisdiction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Discretionary trust anatomy and beneficial-ownership opacity: FINTRAC and Schedule I bank KYC require identification of the settlor, all named beneficiaries or definitive beneficiary classes, the protector, and the trustee; a discretionary asset-protection trust intentionally omitting named remaindermen is an automatic red-flag event under FINTRAC Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Indicators and normally results in account refusal or immediate freezing.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide: (1) a certified true copy of the registered trust deed and any amendments, with a formal trust chronology identifying all endowments and corpus transfers; (2) a Source of Wealth dossier comprising audited financial statements, sale-of-business closing records, probate grants, or long-form tax returns supporting every material contribution; (3) a Source of Funds memorandum tracing the 12-month banking trail underlying each corpus asset; (4) a signed UBO declaration naming the settlor, protector, and each beneficiary class, with FINTRAC-standard KYC forms for any beneficiary holding a fixed remittance interest; (5) CRS and FATCA self-certification documents (Form W-8BEN-E and Canadian CRS Self-Certification) proving whether the ULC is a Reporting or Non-Reporting Financial Institution; and (6) a written legal opinion from Canadian trusts counsel confirming commercial substance, irrevocability, spendthrift protection within Alberta law, and absence of creditor-dissipation intent.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-risk jurisdictional exposure: a non-resident settlor, protector, or investment manager domiciled in FATF-monitored or sanctions-adjacent states, or the routing of contributions through a third-country shell company, triggers enhanced due diligence under PCMLTFA and may mandate mandatory refusal under Bank Act s. 588 and OSFI guidance.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Assemble a Geographic-Risk Explanation File containing: (1) valid passport and renewable residence permit for each authorized signatory; (2) an independent World-Check/Dow Jones or LexisNexis negative-news and sanctions screening report dated within 90 days; (3) three consecutive bank-reference letters from the settlor's primary G-7 or European bank; (4) certified commercial-invoice and trade-contract evidence establishing the economic origin of funds, plus tax-residency certificates for all non-resident parties (Canada NR301 and foreign competent-authority equivalents); (5) a confirmation statement that no director, signatory, or beneficial owner appears on UN, EU, OFAC, or Canadian CPCMLTFA regulated lists; and (6) a written attestation from a Canadian compliance officer that all onward transfers will be blocked against OFAC/CFSIA-listed persons before execution.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Undocumented or split-wired liquidity: repeated wire segments below the C$10,000 FINTRAC threshold, absence of commercial purpose narratives, and fund movement through third-country shell accounts are treated as money-laundering indicators for trusts, resulting in delayed clearance or Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) filing.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Maintain and produce: (1) the engagement letter and trust-administration agreement naming the ULC as fiduciary administrator; (2) a certified payment-instruction register containing the ISO 20022 purpose code for each wire and the explicit narration Trust Distribution — Contingent Beneficiary Tranche or Settlement of Pending Asset Acquisition; (3) bank-source letters from every originating financial institution confirming originator account and ultimate beneficial owner; (4) an investment-management or asset-acquisition ledger reconciling each inflow to a documented commercial or trust obligation; and (5) a board-approved Transactional Justification Memorandum explaining each wire without code words or abbreviations, supported by the seven-year electronic-trial retention required under the PCMLTFA record-keeping provisions.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: All inbound capital injections into the Alberta ULC must be transmitted by SWIFT MT103 single-beneficiary credit transfer from a correspondent bank domiciled in a G-7 or equivalent high-tax jurisdiction, with the beneficiary account identified by its full 15-to-17 digit Canadian account number or applicable IBAN translation. The wire narrative must contain the FINTRAC-compliant reference Treasury Participation — CA_AB_ULC_2025 and the ISO 20022 External Purpose Code B206 for trust and fiduciary services, supported by the underlying trust instrument reference. CAD-denominated funding is settled through the domestic Real-Time Rail or LVTS clearing on the receiving bank's book, while USD-denominated contributions clear through CHIPS or Fedwire via the Canadian bank's US correspondent. Investment Canada Act compliance must be verified: the transaction is outside the review threshold for WTO investors (2025 enterprise-value threshold approximately C$1.33 billion) and the national-security review provisions, but a post-establishment notification under the Investment Canada Act must be filed within 30 days after the ULC becomes non-resident-controlled. Before clearing, the receiving bank will require a statutory wire-release confirmation, a foreign-ownership-control declaration signed by the directors, and a copy of the trust deed naming the ULC as fiduciary.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing rails are: (1) SWIFT MT103 for low-to-mid value single-name payments with priority 300 and two-business-day settlement, supplemented by MT202 COV for transfers that pass through an intermediary financial institution; (2) confirmed irrevocable Commercial Letters of Credit issued and negotiated by Tier-1 Canadian banks under UCP600/eUCP, used for physical-asset and commercial-investment purchases requiring concurrent shipping documents, commercial invoices, and inspection certificates, with strict presentation timelines and the five-banking-day discrepancy-refusal discipline under UCP600 article 14; (3) domestic CAD disbursements over the LVTS/Real-Time Rail; and (4) USD disbursements through the Canadian bank's US correspondent network. Every outbound payment above C$10,000 is subject to mandatory counterparty UBO, PEP, and sanctions screening before execution, and the payment mandate must be signed under the two-signatory rule, with at least one independent or externally appointed Compliance Designated Signatory acceptable to the bank. All disbursements must cite the trust deed reference, the purpose classification (legal fees, independent counsel retainers, auditor fees, beneficiary remittance, or asset-acquisition settlement), and must be logged in the permanent PCMLTFA transaction register.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX Forwards — executed under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a Schedule I Canadian bank for CAD/EUR/USD and other fully convertible pairs, with typical tenors up to 12 months; a Credit Support Annex becomes mandatory when negative mark-to-market exposure exceeds approximately C$100,000.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) — lawfully available for hedging the ULC's receipts or liabilities denominated in restricted emerging-market currencies such as CNY, INR, IDR, BRL, or ARS, because the CAD settlement leg is fully convertible; must be used strictly as a hedge of trustee receipts and never as speculative position-taking, and requires the Canadian bank's commodity-risk and counterparty-credit approval.

Cross-Currency Swaps (CCS) — permitted for matching long-dated USD-denominated settlement liabilities against CAD distributions under an ISDA 2002 CSA; the ULC as a non-financial end-user benefits from the uncleared-margin exemption because its aggregate average notional exposure is far below the in-scope threshold applicable to systemically important financial institutions.

Plain-Vanilla Currency Options (FX puts and calls) — available at Schedule I banks for portfolio protection on large discretionary trust distributions; premiums are payable from the operating account, and no central clearing obligation applies where the option is a transparent hedging instrument covering the ULC's commercial or fiduciary exposure.

FX Swaps (CAD versus USD or EUR for temporary liquidity positioning) — permissible for one-to-three-month tenors with same-day settlement instructions transmitted by MT300 confirmation and monitored under the ULC's board-approved treasury-risk policy.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Alberta Annual Return (annual corporate registration declaration confirming directors and registered office)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry — Service Alberta (filed electronically via authorized service providers)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 calendar days after each anniversary of incorporation or amalgamation; a December 15 incorporation must file by February 13 of the following year annually
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late fee of CAD 100 per overdue year; the Registrar issues a default notice followed by a 60-day cure period; continued non-filing triggers administrative strike-off and dissolution under section 266 of the Alberta Business Corporations Act.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal) including Alberta provincial schedule
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — Calgary or designated Tax Services Office
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after fiscal period end (June 30 for a December 31 year-end); final tax balance remittance due within 2 months after period end (3 months for eligible Canadian-controlled private corporations with an available small-business limit)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty equal to the greater of CAD 100 or 5% of unpaid tax, plus 1% monthly arrears interest for up to 12 months; gross-negligence penalty up to 50% of understated tax; CRA may assess, garnish, and pursue director liability for unpaid statutory amounts.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Alberta corporate income tax declaration (no standalone provincial form; Alberta operates under the Canada–Alberta tax collection agreement)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Ministry of Treasury Board and Finance — administered and collected by CRA
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Synchronized with the federal T2 deadline; Alberta tax liability computed on the federal T2 provincial schedule
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Alberta Corporate Tax Act penalties and prescribed CRA interest on arrears; unpaid Alberta corporate tax may be offset against federal refunds and enforced by garnishment.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual licensed fiduciary supervision renewal, audited financial statements, and AML compliance report under the Alberta Trust Companies Act and PCMLTFA
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Superintendent of Financial Institutions — Treasury Board and Finance; FINTRAC for AML/CTF records
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Audited financial statements and annual AML compliance posture report within 6 months after fiscal year-end; licence renewal on the anniversary date of the fiduciary licence
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Suspension or revocation of the fiduciary licence; cease-and-desist order preventing further administration of asset-protection trusts; administrative monetary penalties; director disqualification; FINTRAC enforcement for AML/CTF deficiencies.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T3 Trust Income Tax Information Return (filed by the ULC in its capacity as trustee for each administered trust that is resident in Canada or earns Canadian-source income)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — Trust Returns Processing
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 90 calendar days after each trust's taxation year-end (March 31 for a December 31 trust year-end)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of CAD 25 per day per T3 return up to a maximum of CAD 2,500 per trust; prescribed interest on unpaid trust taxes; trustee may remain personally liable for penalties arising from trustee default.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit is imposed by the Alberta Trust Companies Act for all licensed fiduciary administrators of third-party trusts; no revenue, asset, or shareholding threshold provides an exemption. Under the Alberta Business Corporations Act the default rule requires appointment of a public accountant at each annual meeting; the unanimous-shareholder audit waiver available for non-public private corporations does not override the licence condition for a regulated fiduciary ULC.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (CPA Canada Handbook Part I) is required for publicly accountable enterprises and is the prevailing framework for licensed trust companies; a private ULC may otherwise adopt ASPE (Part II), but the Alberta Superintendent of Financial Institutions accepts IFRS-based audited statements as the regulatory norm. Statements must be presented in Canadian dollars and audited under Canadian Auditing Standards.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 15% federal general corporate rate + 8% Alberta general rate = 23% combined statutory rate (non-small-business corporations); temporary federal reduction to 14.4% (2024-2025), 13.8% (2026), 14.7% (2027) per 2023 Budget legislation enacted July 2024; Alberta rate unchanged at 8%.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No preferential provincial tax holiday is available in Alberta for fiduciary/trust administration. The 2% Alberta small business rate and 9% federal small business rate on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income apply only to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs); a ULC is disqualified from CCPC status if controlled by non-residents and from the small business deduction where it is not a CCPC — thereby subjected to 23% combined general rate on all taxable income. Federal foreign tax credits (s. 126), the M&P deduction is unavailable for fiduciary fees; investment income tax shelter status absent. ULC retains 'pass-through' eligibility for U.S. check-the-box, but for Canadian tax purposes remains fully taxable as a corporation.
